Question: Who runs NHS hospitals in Scotland, how can a patient complain, what are the complaint stages and response times, and what time limit applies?
NHS hospitals in Scotland are run by the relevant NHS health board. A patient can complain by speaking to staff, contacting the NHS health board by phone, email or online, or writing to the relevant NHS organisation; the stages are first speaking to involved staff, then a senior member of staff or the Feedback and Complaints Officer, then a full written investigation response within 20 working days, and the time limit is normally 6 months from the event or from finding out, but no longer than 12 months after the event itself.

Question: What does this page say about legal aid for adult clinical negligence claims in Scotland, speculative fee agreements/no win no fee, any cap or success fee, and any free advice or scheme support?
The page says legal aid is available in Scotland for all types of clinical negligence cases, including adult claims, but only if the claim has reasonable prospects of success and the applicant passes the financial means test. It says CFA/no win, no fee is available but misleadingly named; any success fee is tapered and capped, so the claimant keeps at least 80% of damages for claims up to £100,000, with higher percentages above that. It also says some firms may meet the ATE insurance cost, and that Avma-approved Scottish clinical negligence solicitors who have signed the Avma Code of Conduct should be able to explain when legal aid might be the best option.

say.text: The hospital route in Scotland starts with the NHS complaint process, and if that does not resolve things you can go to the Scottish Public Services Ombudsman. For injury compensation, Scotland generally uses a court claim for clinical negligence, and the deadline is usually 3 years; for legal help, Scottish Legal Aid Board is the funding body and the Law Society of Scotland directory can help find a solicitor. I could not verify the exact records route or PASS details from quoted pages in this run, so treat those as needing a final check before you act.

steps.what: In Scotland, doctors follow national clinical guidance sponsored and supported by SIGN. SIGN develops evidence-based national clinical practice guidelines.
points: "the development of evidence-based national clinical practice guidelines are sponsored and supported by the Scottish Intercollegiate Guidelines Network (SIGN)"
"SIGN is part of the Evidence Directorate of Healthcare Improvement Scotland"
"Its objective is to improve the quality of health care for patients in Scotland by reducing variation in practice and outcome"

sources.quote: In Scotland, the development of evidence-based national clinical practice guidelines are sponsored and supported by the Scottish Intercollegiate Guidelines Network (SIGN), which was established by the Academy of Royal Colleges in 1993.

Its objective is to improve the quality of health care for patients in Scotland by reducing variation in practice and outcome, through the development and dissemination of national clinical guidelines containing recommendations for effective practice based on current evidence.

takeaway.why: The development of evidence-based national clinical practice guidelines are sponsored and supported by SIGN.

AvMA says Scotland is one of the regions in its solicitor search, but it explains that it does not accredit specialist medical negligence solicitors there. It says: “There is a different legal system in Scotland and Ireland to England & Wales, and Avma does not accredit specialist medical negligence solicitors in Scotland and Ireland.”

No. The page lists NHS Lothian’s complaints contact information, but it does not show a separate entry for Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh specifically. It does link to the relevant NHS Lothian complaints handling procedure.

NHS hospitals in Scotland are run by the relevant NHS health board. A patient can complain by speaking to staff, contacting the NHS health board by phone, email or online, or writing to the relevant NHS organisation; the stages are first speaking to involved staff, then a senior member of staff or the Feedback and Complaints Officer, then a full written investigation response within 20 working days, and the time limit is normally 6 months from the event or from finding out, but no longer than 12 months after the event itself.
This page does not say what body publishes the clinical guidance doctors follow, and it does not mention NICE or what it is for.

This page does not give the official complaint process details you asked for. It only says to get information on how to complain from NHS inform, get help from PASS, and complain to the Scottish Public Service Ombudsman (SPSO) if you're unhappy with the NHS response.

The page says legal aid is available in Scotland for all types of clinical negligence cases, including adult claims, but only if the claim has reasonable prospects of success and the applicant passes the financial means test. It says CFA/no win, no fee is available but misleadingly named; any success fee is tapered and capped, so the claimant keeps at least 80% of damages for claims up to £100,000, with higher percentages above that. It also says some firms may meet the ATE insurance cost, and that Avma-approved Scottish clinical negligence solicitors who have signed the Avma Code of Conduct should be able to explain when legal aid might be the best option.

The PDF says you may be able to get public funding/legal aid if you are on a low income, and your solicitor will help assess eligibility. It also says specialist firms may fund the claim on a written speculative fee agreement (no-win no-fee), but you may still have to pay for some initial investigations and insurance may be needed for the other side’s costs if you lose. Most specialist solicitors offer free initial advice, and all solicitors must tell you in writing what their fees and outlays will be.

The Patient Advice and Support Service (PASS) is provided by Citizens Advice Bureaux in Scotland. It is an independent service that gives free, confidential information, advice and support to anyone who uses the NHS in Scotland.

This page explains who to complain to for different NHS services, but it does not give the stages or response times for the NHS complaints procedure. It also does not say what happens if the response is not good enough.

The page says clinical negligence claims can be funded by legal aid, in which case the Scottish Legal Aid Board pays the costs. It also says a claim may be investigated on a ‘no win, no fee’ basis with an independent insurer paying outlays and taking the litigation risk, while the funder takes a percentage of any compensation recovered. The firm says it would not encourage privately funded claims because they are complex and involve risk, though private funding is not ruled out.

The page says local NHS complaints advocacy services are free and independent, and they can help people make a complaint about the NHS, compose letters, and accompany them to meetings. It also says they are commissioned and financed by local authorities across England, and an NHS advocate may speak to other agencies on a person's behalf, such as Avma.

The page says the Scottish Intercollegiate Guidelines Network (SIGN) supports and sponsors national clinical practice guidelines in Scotland. The exact wording is: “the development of evidence-based national clinical practice guidelines are sponsored and supported by the Scottish Intercollegiate Guidelines Network (SIGN)”.

Clinical guidance: Scottish Intercollegiate Guidelines Network (SIGN). In Scotland, doctors follow national clinical guidance sponsored and supported by SIGN. SIGN develops evidence-based national clinical practice guidelines.

PASS says everyone has the right to access their medical record, but some parts may be redacted for safety reasons. You need to contact your hospital and/or GP, be specific about the time period if possible, and one copy is free while further copies incur a fee. If requesting someone else’s record, you generally need power of attorney; for a child an authorised adult can apply, and for a deceased person you must be a personal representative, administrator, or executor and submit a Subject Access Request Form with proof of identity and relationship.

Free help: Patient Advice and Support Service (PASS). PASS gives free, independent, confidential information, advice and support to anyone who uses the NHS in Scotland. It is provided by Citizens Advice Bureaux in Scotland. (one official source)

Paying for help: Scottish Legal Aid Board. Adults in Scotland can get legal aid for clinical negligence claims if the case has reasonable prospects of success and they pass the financial means test. A solicitor can also act under a no win, no fee speculative fee agreement, and most specialist solicitors offer free initial advice. (one official source)

The page says Scotland had not yet decided on a no-fault compensation scheme; the consultation was to gather views on whether one should be introduced and what its scope should be. It says the Scottish Government saw no-fault compensation as a favored way forward, but also noted the need to work through practical implications and costs. The problems discussed are delays in court-based claims and legal fees, and the alternatives mentioned are the existing clinical negligence arrangements and a limited scheme for neurologically impaired infants, with the Swedish model cited as an example.

They recommend “Find Clinical Negligence Solicitors at The Law Society of Scotland” and also link to “Find a Solicitor | Law Society of Scotland.” The exact wording about specialist clinical negligence solicitors is: “You should consult a specialist Clinical Negligence Solicitor if you want to take legal action.”
It says the main legal time limit is that court proceedings must be started within 3 years of the negligence happening or coming to light. For children, the limit is by the child's 19th birthday.

The procedure has two complaint stages: stage one is early resolution, and stage two is investigation. The page states that a concern should be responded to within five working days, and it refers to timelines and extensions for the complaint stages, but it does not give the specific complaint-stage response times or all time limits on this page. It also says that if a matter is handled as a complaint after being a concern, it should go directly to the investigation stage.
